H1.original: Small sample size needs augmentation and robustness checking
H1.statement: The analysis rests on a small sample, which needs to be augmented with additional data and subjected to robustness checks, since the results may not hold up without them.

H2.original:
BK’s main results are calculated using a regression of around 50 observations. The regression appears to have at least 7 parameters.
...not clear that the asymptotic approximations required to justify their frequentist confidence intervals are appropriate.
H2.statement: The main results of BK come from a regression with around 50 observations that appears to have at least 7 parameters. With so few observations relative to parameters, it is unclear that the asymptotic approximations needed to justify the frequentist confidence intervals are appropriate.

H3.original: I would suggest providing simulation evidence to illustrate the validity of their confidence regions in their setting, with time series data, few observations, and lots of parameters.
H3.statement: The paper should provide simulation evidence showing whether its confidence regions are valid in its setting, which combines time series data, few observations, and many parameters. Without such evidence, the validity of the reported confidence regions is not established.

H4.original: Authors responded (September 2025) by introducing the BU dataset, which spans 160 years. human evaluator note they performed inference robustness using bootstrapping techniques in the appendix.
H4.statement: The paper introduces a BU dataset spanning 160 years and reports inference robustness using bootstrapping techniques in an appendix, which addresses the concern about small sample size.

H5.original:
Consider longer-term effects
human evaluator: “It would be good to show the impacts for more than 10 years out, and to include a robustness check SCC calculation which allows for longer run effects”
[human evaluator] . The revised paper directly addresses this by converting their estimates to the damage implied by a permanent 1°C rise in temperature, yielding the much larger long-run figure of 22–34% GDP reduction.
Sept version “In the longer BU sample, the same temperature shock leads to a peak effect at 18% after 5 years with a 95% confidence interval of (6%, 30%), ...  In both cases, impacts do not fully mean-revert even after 10 years. “
And it explicitly includes a section on Sensitivity that details how the SCC changes under alternative assumptions
H5.statement: The analysis reports impacts only up to 10 years ahead, and the critique asks for longer-term effects and a robustness SCC calculation that allows for longer-run effects. The paper converts its estimates to the damage implied by a permanent 1°C rise in temperature, yielding a long-run GDP reduction of 22–34%, and in the longer BU sample a peak effect of 18% after 5 years with a 95% confidence interval of (6%, 30%), with impacts not fully mean-reverting after 10 years. A sensitivity section reports how the SCC changes under alternative assumptions.

[human evaluator]:  human evaluator requested increasing the number of lags, especially given the longer cycles noted in geoscience. The newer version notes that in the longer BU sample, they use 4 to 8 lags to capture the complexity of the historical series.
Less important, I guess
Non-Linear Effects and Comparability:
NotebookLM:  human evaluator requested allowing the local temperature model to include non-linear or permanent growth effects for a fair comparison with previous literature. While the authors maintain their main conservative assumption of level effects (not permanent growth effects), they clarify that their local temperature estimates generate a 3% long-run GDP reduction, which is consistent with the "level effects" benchmark of the conventional literature. They explicitly report that imposing non-linear specifications on their shocks did not materially change the core estimates.
Out-of-Sample Extrapolation: human evaluator suggested acknowledging how far out of sample the 1°C calibration is, given that shocks are typically around 0.3°C. The 2025 version notes that scaling up to a 1°C increase requires assuming linearity, thereby explicitly addressing this methodological limitation, although they suggest that the consistency of their linear estimates across shock sizes supports the approach.
H6.statement: The critique asks for more lags, given the longer cycles noted in geoscience, and the paper now uses 4 to 8 lags in the longer BU sample to capture the complexity of the historical series. It also asks that the local temperature model allow non-linear or permanent growth effects for comparison with the previous literature, and the paper keeps its level-effects assumption, reporting a 3% long-run GDP reduction consistent with the conventional level-effects benchmark, with non-linear specifications not materially changing the core estimates. Finally, the critique notes that the 1°C calibration is far out of sample relative to shocks of about 0.3°C, and the paper acknowledges that scaling to 1°C requires assuming linearity, arguing that consistency of linear estimates across shock sizes supports the approach.
